screens.title: Introduction to Local Data Storage
screens.narratorSegment: Local data storage is a practical tool every mobile developer uses to make apps feel reliable and personal. In this lesson you will learn when to choose lightweight device storage, and why shared_preferences is a solid fit for small pieces of state like user preferences, a remembered city, or a high score. We will treat shared_preferences as a key-value sticky note pad: you give each value a unique string key and store primitives such as strings, integers, booleans, doubles, or small lists of strings. That design keeps your app responsive because these operations are small and easy to reason about. You will also see how these calls are asynchronous, why you must await them, and why complex objects or secrets are not suitable for this A P I without serialization or encryption. Throughout the chapter you will examine concrete code examples for adding the dependency, reading and writing a boolean setting, and the common mistakes beginners make, like forgetting to await writes. By the end you should be able to choose shared_preferences for the right use cases and avoid common traps that lead to stale data or insecure storage. Which small piece of state in your app could you store locally first?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction to Local Data Storage
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to Local Data Storage

Practical patterns for storing small, persistent values on-device using shared_preferences in Flutter.

In this lesson

Understand when to use local persistence, add shared_preferences, read and write primitive data, and avoid common mistakes.

Why it matters

Small persistent values make apps feel personal and reliable even offline, while keeping complexity low compared to full databases.

Explore Key Topics
Purpose
Store user settings and small caches without a database.
shared_preferences
A simple key-value API for primitive types.
Async
Reads and writes return futures; always await to avoid race conditions.
Concept Map

Key pieces of local persistence

Use cases

Remember preferences, store last-viewed item, cache small results for offline use.

Limitations

Not for large datasets, relational queries, or unencrypted secrets.

Types

String, int, bool, double, and List are supported directly.

Async behavior

Get instance and set operations return futures—await them to ensure completion.

This slide orients you to what we'll cover: dependency setup, reading and writing, handling async, serialization, and practical examples.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will know when to choose local device storage, how to add and use shared_preferences, how to handle asynchronous reads and writes, and how to spot common mistakes. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters. First, you will recognize appropriate use cases for small persistent values like preferences or a cached selection. Second, you will set up the shared_preferences dependency and read or write primitive data. Third, you will distinguish synchronous thinking from asynchronous code that returns futures and learn to await operations so your UI stays consistent. Fourth, you will learn best practices such as using default values, keeping keys unique, serializing objects when needed, and avoiding storage of sensitive data without encryption. These objectives are intentionally practical: they map directly to tasks you will implement in code and tests, and they reduce the chance of bugs caused by race conditions or incorrect storage choices. Think about a small preference in your app you could persist as you follow these objectives.

screens.title: What is local data persistence?
screens.narratorSegment: Local data persistence means storing application state or small pieces of data on the device itself so they survive app restarts and sometimes offline usage. It is different from a remote database in that it's intended for lightweight storage: a few settings, a remembered selection, or small cached content. A concrete example is storing a user's preferred temperature unit in a weather app. When the user picks Celsius, the app saves that choice locally so the next time it opens, it shows Celsius immediately without waiting for a network call. Another example is a game's high score. Keeping such values locally improves perceived performance and makes the app functional when connectivity is absent. A common misconception is that all persistent data must be stored in a database; that's not true. Databases are appropriate for complex, relational, or large datasets. Local persistence via key-value storage is simpler to implement, simpler to reason about, and often more efficient for small items. Always ask: does the data need structure, queries, or encryption? If not, a simple local store is likely the right choice. What tiny piece of state in your app would benefit from being remembered this way?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is local data persistence?
Definition

Storing small pieces of state on the device so they persist across app restarts and can be used offline.

Example: Weather app

Remember temperature unit or last-viewed city so the app shows relevant data immediately on launch.

Example: Game

Persist a high score locally so it remains available offline and after restarts.

Common misconception

Local storage must be a database. In fact, for simple pairs a key-value store is faster and much simpler to maintain.

Key Takeaway

Use local persistence for small, non-sensitive values that improve UX and work offline.

When not to use it
  • Large datasets or complex relationships that require queries.
  • Sensitive secrets like passwords unless encrypted with secure storage.
  • When you need server-wide consistency or centralized sync.
Quick checks
Is it small?
Yes: key-value is fine.
Is it sensitive?
Yes: do not use shared_preferences alone.

screens.title: shared_preferences: a key-value store
screens.narratorSegment: shared_preferences is a Flutter package that exposes a persistent key-value store for simple data types. It maps string keys to primitive values such as strings, integers, booleans, doubles, and lists of strings. This makes it ideal for small settings or small lists of values. The A P I is intentionally minimal: you fetch a singleton instance and call setter and getter methods like setBool, getBool, setString, getStringList, or setInt. A useful pattern is to choose descriptive keys so your code remains readable and to consolidate keys in a constants file. Because the package stores only primitive values, you cannot directly save a custom object. Instead serialize that object to a JSON string and store the string. When reading, deserialize it back into your object. This is an explicit design decision: keep the storage simple and leave complex models to databases or structured files. Remember that this A P I is not encrypted by default, so avoid saving secrets here. Use shared_preferences for lightweight, low-risk data that enhances UX without requiring complex queries. shared_preferences: a key-value store means a minimal persistent map from string keys to primitive values for simple, local app state.. In practical terms, what the package stores and its supported types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Add the dependency and get the package
screens.narratorSegment: Adding shared_preferences to your Flutter project is a simple, deliberate process that ensures the package is available to your code. First, edit pubspec. yaml to include the dependency under dependencies. Then run flutter pub get in a terminal to fetch and lock the package version. This step integrates the native implementations for Android and iOS so the plugin can persist data on each platform. After fetching, you can import the package in your Dart files. A common mistake is to add the dependency and not run the package manager, which leads to missing import errors. Another small pitfall is pinning an out-of-date version; prefer a recent stable release line. Finally, understand that adding the dependency does not automatically alter behavior — you must obtain the SharedPreferences instance in code and call methods to store or retrieve values. This setup flow keeps your project reproducible and ensures team members get the same package version when they run the project. screens.title: Getting and using SharedPreferences
screens.narratorSegment: To interact with the shared_preferences store you first obtain a SharedPreferences instance. This retrieval is asynchronous and returns a future that completes with a singleton tied to the platform-specific backing store. Always await this call before reading or writing values. Once you have the instance, use typed set methods like setBool or setString and matching get methods to read them back. A pattern to follow is to read settings in initState of a stateful widget, using a default when the key is absent. For writes, await set calls so you know the operation completed. A typical mistake is not awaiting a set call before navigating away or closing the app; that can cause data loss. Also note that get methods return nullable types when a key is missing, so use null coalescing to provide safe defaults. The code panel on this slide shows a minimal example for loading and toggling a boolean setting; study how the instance is awaited and how set and get are used with defaults. Getting and using SharedPreferences means await sharedpreferences.getinstance(), then use setx/getx methods and provide defaults for missing keys.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Getting and using SharedPreferences
Minimal pattern
Future _loadSettings() async {
  final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  final isDark = prefs.getBool('isDarkMode') ?? false;
  setState(() => _isDarkMode = isDark);
}

Future _toggleDarkMode(bool value) async {
  setState(() => _isDarkMode = value);
  final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  await prefs.setBool('isDarkMode', value);
}
Notice getBool returns null when the key is missing, so we use ?? false to provide a safe default. Also notice we await setBool to ensure the write completes.
Explanation bullets
  • getInstance is async; await it to get the singleton tied to persistent storage.
  • Typed getters can return null; provide defaults with the null-coalescing operator.
  • Always await set calls to avoid race conditions and potential data loss.
Key Takeaway

Treat shared_preferences calls as asynchronous and provide defaults for missing keys to keep UI consistent.

screens.title: Practical example: Dark mode setting
screens.narratorSegment: This example demonstrates a complete pattern for storing a boolean preference for dark mode. The widget loads persisted settings in initState by awaiting SharedPreferences. getInstance and reading a boolean with a default if the key is missing. When the user toggles dark mode, the state is updated immediately for a responsive UI and the change is then written to disk with await prefs. setBool. This order—update UI first, then persist—keeps the app feeling fast while ensuring the value is saved. Also notice we use descriptive keys like isDarkMode which makes later debugging and refactoring easier. A common misconception is to assume writes are instantaneous; because they are asynchronous you must await them, especially if the app may close or navigate away right after. If you need to ensure persistence before navigation, await the write before proceeding. This pattern balances user experience with data safety and is appropriate for many small preferences. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Dark mode example
Example code
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

class SettingsScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const SettingsScreen({super.key});

  @override
  State<SettingsScreen> createState() => _SettingsScreenState();
}

class _SettingsScreenState extends State<SettingsScreen> {
  bool _isDarkMode = false;
  final String _darkModeKey = 'isDarkMode';

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _loadSettings();
  }

  Future<void> _loadSettings() async {
    final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
    setState(() {
      _isDarkMode = prefs.getBool(_darkModeKey) ?? false;
    });
  }

  Future<void> _toggleDarkMode(bool value) async {
    setState(() { _isDarkMode = value; });
    final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
    await prefs.setBool(_darkModeKey, _isDarkMode);
  }
}
Notes
  • Load values in initState to initialize UI before user interaction.
  • Update state first for responsiveness, then persist with await.
  • Use descriptive keys and defaults to prevent null issues.
Misconception

Writes always finish instantly. In reality you should await writes if subsequent logic depends on persistence.

screens.title: When not to use shared_preferences
screens.narratorSegment: shared_preferences is excellent for small key-value needs, but it has clear trade-offs. Use it for preferences, simple flags, and tiny caches. When your data needs structure, querying, relations, or large volume, a local database like SQLite or a higher-level ORM is a better fit. For sensitive information, shared_preferences is not encrypted by default, so consider secure platform storage or encrypted databases. A helpful way to decide is to compare along three axes: data shape, size, and sensitivity. If the data shape is primitive, size is small, and sensitivity is low, shared_preferences is a good choice. But if you need relationships, transactions, or robust querying, choose a database. If you need to protect secrets such as tokens or passwords, choose secure storage. A common beginner error is to try to store lists of complex objects directly; instead serialize them to JSON strings or migrate to a database for richer models. This comparison helps you pick the right tool for maintainable, secure storage. When not to use shared_preferences means key-value stores are simple and fast for small data; databases and secure storage are better for complex, large, or sensitive data.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › When not to use shared_preferences
Comparison table
shared_preferences
Best for small primitives, fast setup, not encrypted, no queries.
Local database (SQLite)
Structured data, queries, relationships, larger volumes, more complexity to maintain.
Secure storage
Encrypted platform-backed storage for secrets and tokens; use for sensitive data.
Decision checklist
  • Is the item primitive and small? → shared_preferences.
  • Does it require queries or relations? → database.
  • Is it sensitive? → secure storage or encryption.
Common mistake

Choosing shared_preferences because it is easy, even when the data model will soon outgrow it; plan for migration.

screens.title: Best practices and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Following a few best practices will save you debugging time when using shared_preferences. First, centralize your keys as constants so they remain consistent across your codebase and are easy to refactor. Second, always provide default values when reading keys to avoid null exceptions and unpredictable UI. fullNarratorScript:
Local data storage is a practical tool every mobile developer uses to make apps feel reliable and personal. In this lesson you will learn when to choose lightweight device storage, and why shared_preferences is a solid fit for small pieces of state like user preferences, a remembered city, or a high score. We will treat shared_preferences as a key-value sticky note pad: you give each value a unique string key and store primitives such as strings, integers, booleans, doubles, or small lists of strings. That design keeps your app responsive because these operations are small and easy to reason about. You will also see how these calls are asynchronous, why you must await them, and why complex objects or secrets are not suitable for this A P I without serialization or encryption. Throughout the chapter you will examine concrete code examples for adding the dependency, reading and writing a boolean setting, and the common mistakes beginners make, like forgetting to await writes. By the end you should be able to choose shared_preferences for the right use cases and avoid common traps that lead to stale data or insecure storage. Which small piece of state in your app could you store locally first?

By the end of these screens you will know when to choose local device storage, how to add and use shared_preferences, how to handle asynchronous reads and writes, and how to spot common mistakes. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters. First, you will recognize appropriate use cases for small persistent values like preferences or a cached selection. Second, you will set up the shared_preferences dependency and read or write primitive data. Third, you will distinguish synchronous thinking from asynchronous code that returns futures and learn to await operations so your UI stays consistent. Fourth, you will learn best practices such as using default values, keeping keys unique, serializing objects when needed, and avoiding storage of sensitive data without encryption. These objectives are intentionally practical: they map directly to tasks you will implement in code and tests, and they reduce the chance of bugs caused by race conditions or incorrect storage choices. Think about a small preference in your app you could persist as you follow these objectives.

These applied objectives show what you will actually do in code and when testing. You will add the shared_preferences dependency to pubspec. yaml and run the package manager, which ensures the A P I is available in your project. You will write code to obtain a SharedPreferences instance and use set and get methods for booleans, strings, integers, doubles, and lists of strings. In tests or manual checks you will verify defaults by handling nulls with fallback values so your app behaves predictably on first run. You will practice serializing simple objects to JSON strings when a list or small object is needed. Lastly, you will write code that awaits writes before closing or moving on to reduce the risk of data loss. Each applied step reduces runtime bugs and gives you reliable, testable behavior for settings and small persisted lists.

Local data persistence means storing application state or small pieces of data on the device itself so they survive app restarts and sometimes offline usage. It is different from a remote database in that it's intended for lightweight storage: a few settings, a remembered selection, or small cached content. A concrete example is storing a user's preferred temperature unit in a weather app. When the user picks Celsius, the app saves that choice locally so the next time it opens, it shows Celsius immediately without waiting for a network call. Another example is a game's high score. Keeping such values locally improves perceived performance and makes the app functional when connectivity is absent. A common misconception is that all persistent data must be stored in a database; that's not true. Databases are appropriate for complex, relational, or large datasets. Local persistence via key-value storage is simpler to implement, simpler to reason about, and often more efficient for small items. Always ask: does the data need structure, queries, or encryption? If not, a simple local store is likely the right choice. What tiny piece of state in your app would benefit from being remembered this way?

shared_preferences is a Flutter package that exposes a persistent key-value store for simple data types. It maps string keys to primitive values such as strings, integers, booleans, doubles, and lists of strings. This makes it ideal for small settings or small lists of values. The A P I is intentionally minimal: you fetch a singleton instance and call setter and getter methods like setBool, getBool, setString, getStringList, or setInt. A useful pattern is to choose descriptive keys so your code remains readable and to consolidate keys in a constants file. Because the package stores only primitive values, you cannot directly save a custom object. Instead serialize that object to a JSON string and store the string. When reading, deserialize it back into your object. This is an explicit design decision: keep the storage simple and leave complex models to databases or structured files. Remember that this A P I is not encrypted by default, so avoid saving secrets here. Use shared_preferences for lightweight, low-risk data that enhances UX without requiring complex queries. shared_preferences: a key-value store means a minimal persistent map from string keys to primitive values for simple, local app state.. Adding shared_preferences to your Flutter project is a simple, deliberate process that ensures the package is available to your code. First, edit pubspec. yaml to include the dependency under dependencies. Then run flutter pub get in a terminal to fetch and lock the package version. This step integrates the native implementations for Android and iOS so the plugin can persist data on each platform. After fetching, you can import the package in your Dart files. A common mistake is to add the dependency and not run the package manager, which leads to missing import errors. Another small pitfall is pinning an out-of-date version; prefer a recent stable release line. Finally, understand that adding the dependency does not automatically alter behavior — you must obtain the SharedPreferences instance in code and call methods to store or retrieve values. This setup flow keeps your project reproducible and ensures team members get the same package version when they run the project.
